title: Operational Requirements (Retrenchment) — Organisational Process Flow
subtitle: Sections 189 and 189A of the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 · Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (GN 3470, GG 53294), Part G, items 22–24 and Annexure A · Facilitation Regulations under s.189A(6) · As at 19 October 2026

overview.summary: This flow tells an employer what to do, by when, and who hands off to whom, from the moment management first sees that jobs may be at risk for business reasons until the last referral window closes and lessons feed back into policy. It runs one shared spine for every retrenchment, then splits at the point where the law splits:

notes.text: Every case moves through the same phases: readiness; identifying the need and choosing the route; the s.189(3) notice and disclosure; consultation on the track that applies; decision, selection and notice of termination; termination and aftercare; and governance. The flow assumes no collective agreement or bargaining council agreement regulates retrenchment procedure; where one does, it prevails and this flow must be adjusted.

notes.heading: Legal status
notes.text: The fairness of a dismissal for operational requirements is governed by the LRA: s.188(1)(a)(ii) (fair reason), s.188(1)(b) (fair procedure), s.189 (procedure for all employers), s.189A (additional rules for large-scale dismissals by employers with more than 50 employees), s.191 (dispute routes) and s.192 (onus on the employer once dismissal is proved). “Operational requirements” means requirements based on the economic, technological, structural or similar needs of an employer (s.213). The Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (“the Code”), issued under s.203 and in effect from 4 September 2025, repealed both the Schedule 8 Code and the separate Code of Good Practice on Dismissal Based on Operational Requirements (1999). It is guidance, not statute, but anyone deciding whether a dismissal was fair must take it into account (s.188(2), s.203(3)). Item references verified against the final Code (GN 3470, GG 53294, 4 September 2025): Part G items 22–24, footnote 7 and Annexure A items 1–9 match the citations in this flow. Severance is governed by the BCEA (s.41), and notice by BCEA s.37–38. A search on 29 September 2026 (rechecked at the 15 October 2026 review) found no enacted amendment to ss.189 or 189A since 2014 and none to the Code since publication. A draft Labour Relations Amendment Bill (published for comment 26 February 2026, not yet tabled) proposes deleting s.189A(13)–(18) and other changes to s.189A; it is not law (DRAFT). Monitor under 6.6.

notes.heading: Labels used throughout
points: LRA = the Labour Relations Act and other statutes and regulations (BCEA, EEA, Facilitation Regulations, POPIA, Companies Act, Insolvency Act); binding now.
Code = the Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (cited by item number); must be taken into account, and departures must be justified.
CL = a principle from case law, cited by name, court and year. Verify the citation and any later authority before using it in advice.
BP = best practice or internal control; not a statutory deadline. Adopt as policy so it becomes binding internally.

notes.heading: Design principle
notes.text: Retrenchment is a no-fault dismissal with a high human cost (Code item 22(3)), so the law puts the burden on the employer to show a genuine and fair business reason, that dismissal was a last resort, and that it consulted with an open mind before deciding (Code items 23(2)–(3), 24(5)–(6)). The flow is built so that every later challenge can be answered from a record made at the time: the business case written as a proposal, the notice, the disclosure log, the minutes, the written replies to written representations, the alternatives register and the selection matrix. The statutory clock starts on the date of the s.189(3) notice; the internal clock starts earlier, when management first contemplates job losses. Internal targets sit inside every statutory limit.

notes.heading: Ten interpretation points that shape the flow
points: The weight of the Code. The Code is intentionally general; departures may be justified in proper circumstances, including the size of the establishment (item 2(1)); it does not alter rights under a collective agreement (item 2(3)); and it must not be read as requiring small businesses to do what is impractical (item 3). Guidance that was only in the repealed 1999 operational requirements code (for example on bumping, LIFO and social plans) now survives only as case law and best practice. Record any justified departure at the time.

s.189A adds to s.189; it never replaces it. Every large-scale retrenchment must still meet every requirement of s.189(1)–(7). Section 189A adds a threshold, a minimum timetable, the facilitation option, the right to strike over the dismissals, and a different procedural remedy. This is why the flow runs one spine with three tracks rather than two separate processes.

The threshold test. Section 189A applies only to an employer employing more than 50 employees that contemplates dismissing at least 10 (up to 200 employees), 20 (201–300), 30 (301–400), 40 (401–500) or 50 (more than 500) employees, or where the number contemplated plus the number dismissed for operational requirements in the 12 months before the s.189(3) notice equals or exceeds that number (s.189A(1)). The employer is the legal entity, not the group (public service: the executing authority, s.189A(20)). The Act does not say on what date headcount is measured or whether TES workers deemed to be employees under s.198A(3)(b) count. Take a dated headcount on the notice date, include deemed TES employees, and where the answer is borderline or numbers may grow, treat the matter as s.189A (BP). If the number contemplated rises above the threshold during consultation, take advice on issuing a fresh notice.

“Contemplates” means before the decision. Consultation must start when the employer contemplates dismissal, not after it has decided (s.189(1)). An employer may have a preferred proposal, but must keep an open mind and seriously consider every proposal (Code item 24(6); CL: Atlantis Diesel Engines v NUMSA, AD 1995; Johnson & Johnson v CWIU, LAC 1998). Board papers, investor announcements and internal emails must speak of a proposal to consult, not a decision to dismiss.

Fair reason: genuine and fair. The reason and the selection must both relate to operational requirements (Code item 23(1)). A court asks whether the reason is genuine and whether dismissal was a fair response in the light of the alternatives, not only whether a commercial rationale exists (CL: BMD Knitting Mills v SACTWU, LAC 2001; CWIU v Algorax, LAC 2003). Retrenching to improve profitability, not only to survive, can be fair (CL: General Food Industries v FAWU, LAC 2004). Note that Code item 23(2) describes dismissal as a measure of last resort; in profit-improvement cases, record why each alternative could not achieve the objective. Dismissing employees who refuse changes to terms is not automatically unfair if the dismissal is genuinely for operational reasons and final, rather than a device to compel acceptance of a demand (s.187(1)(c); CL: NUMSA v Aveng Trident Steel, CC 2020).

Who must be consulted. Section 189(1) sets a hierarchy: first anyone the employer must consult under a collective agreement; if none, a workplace forum (for affected employees in its workplace) and any registered union whose members are likely to be affected; if no workplace forum, the registered union; if no union, the affected employees or their nominated representatives. Apply the hierarchy per affected employee, so that unionised and non-unionised employees are both covered. Bargaining council agreements may regulate the process (Code item 24(4) footnote).

Counting days. LRA periods are calendar days, excluding the first and including the last, unless the last is a Sunday or public holiday (Interpretation Act 33 of 1957 s.4). The 60 days in s.189A(7) and the 30 days in s.189A(8)(a) run from the date the s.189(3) notice was given (day 0). Because the statute requires the periods to “have elapsed” or “lapsed”, the earliest s.189A(8)(a) referral is day 31 and the earliest s.189A(7) termination notice is day 61 (60 full days must have elapsed after the notice date). The Labour Court Rules, 2024 (in operation from 17 July 2024, verify) exclude 16 December to 15 January from “days” for court time limits only; do not apply that exclusion to LRA periods.

Different dispute routes. For a s.189-only dismissal, both procedure and reason go to the CCMA or a council within 30 days, then to the Labour Court (s.191(5)(b)(ii)), or to arbitration where s.191(12) applies (individual consultation, only that employee dismissed, or an employer whose workforce is fewer than ten employees, verify current wording). For a s.189A dismissal, procedural complaints can be raised only by a s.189A(13) application within 30 days of the notice of termination (s.189A(17)); the Labour Court may not decide procedural fairness in a s.191 referral (s.189A(18)); and the substantive dispute goes to the Labour Court or is pursued by strike, but not both (s.189A(10)) (CL: Steenkamp v Edcon, CC 2016; Steenkamp v Edcon [2019] ZACC 17 (CC)). After failed facilitation the substantive dispute goes directly to the Labour Court without conciliation (CL: NUMSA v Industrial Oleo Chemical Products [2026] ZACC 22).

Premature notice does not make a dismissal invalid. Notice of termination given before the s.189A(7) or (8) periods expire is a procedural defect: it entitles the union to strike (s.189A(9)) and exposes the employer to s.189A(13) orders, but the dismissal is not void (CL: Steenkamp v Edcon, CC 2016, which rejected the invalidity line in the LAC decisions in De Beers and Revan (verify full citations)). Treat the periods as hard floors all the same.

Who is the employer. A temporary employment service is the employer of placed workers, but after three months below-threshold workers performing temporary services are deemed employees of the client (s.198A(3)(b); CL: Assign Services v NUMSA, CC 2018); ending a placement to avoid deeming is a dismissal (s.198A(4)). In a transfer of a going concern, dismissal because of the transfer is automatically unfair (s.187(1)(g)). In business rescue, retrenchments remain subject to ss.189 and 189A (Companies Act s.136(1)(b)); on sequestration or liquidation, contracts are suspended (Insolvency Act s.38(1)); the trustee or liquidator must consult before terminating (s.38(5)–(7), proposals within 21 days); suspended contracts end 45 days after the final appointment unless agreed otherwise (s.38(9)); BCEA s.41(2) severance applies.

notes.heading: Roles used
notes.text: Employee Relations Officer (ERO, the process owner and spine; in smaller organisations the HR manager); Senior Sign-off (SSO, e.g. CEO or COO; the Board where material); Board or Remuneration / Social and Ethics Committee (BOARD); Legal Adviser (LA); Finance (FIN); Line Management (LM); HR Manager (HR); Payroll (PAY); Benefits Administrator (BEN); Communications (COMMS); Employer consultation team (ECT: SSO delegate, ERO, FIN and LM representatives). Consulting parties (CP): trade union (TU), workplace forum (WF), nominated employee representatives (REP). Affected employees (EMP). External: CCMA or council (CCMA/BC); facilitator (FAC); Labour Court (LC); Unemployment Insurance Fund (UIF); South African Revenue Service (SARS); retirement fund or insurer (FUND); temporary employment service (TES); business rescue practitioner (BRP).

notes.heading: Employee side of Phase 0
notes.text: Nothing is owed yet, but the fairness of selection is decided here: criteria applied to inaccurate service or skills data are neither fair nor objective.

stages.title: Common steps (all tracks)
intro: Consultation is a meaningful joint consensus-seeking process on the s.189(2) topics: measures to avoid dismissals, minimise their number, change their timing and mitigate their effects; the selection method; and severance (s.189(2); Code item 24(5)–(7)). The employer must allow representations on these and any other related matter, consider and respond to them, give reasons for disagreeing, and reply in writing to written representations (s.189(5)–(6)). The common steps below apply on every track; the track tables add what differs.

intro: Annexure A item 9 tells only employers with more than 50 employees to disclose total headcount and op-req dismissals in the preceding 12 months, but s.189(3)(i)–(j) require every employer to disclose them. Follow the Act.
Item 24(4) omits the workplace forum and nominated representatives, though item 24(3) cross-refers to all s.189(1) parties; follow s.189(1).
Code item 24(7) lists the consultation topics, but does not repeat the s.189(6) duty to respond in writing to written representations, the most commonly breached requirement.

The Code gives no guidance on bumping, LIFO and its exceptions, voluntary packages, TES workers, the s.189A threshold count, what “contemplates” means, or facilitation, much of which the repealed 1999 code covered.

Annexure A footnote 8 suggests giving full names, job titles and numbers of affected employees in the notice. That can make the process look pre-decided and raises POPIA questions; the Act requires numbers and job categories (s.189(3)(c)).
s.189A(1) does not fix the date on which the “more than 50 employees” count is taken or say whether deemed TES employees count.
s.189A(8)(b) makes notice of termination depend on the s.64(1)(a) period having elapsed, but that period only runs after a referral. The Act does not say what happens if no party refers.

s.189A(7)(b)(ii) refers to a Labour Court referral “in terms of section 191(11)”, which runs from a conciliation certificate, while Facilitation Regulations reg 9 runs 90 days from the termination notice. After failed facilitation, a dispute about the fairness of the reason goes directly to the Labour Court within 90 days of the termination notice; conciliation is not required (CL: NUMSA v Industrial Oleo Chemical Products [2026] ZACC 22, overruling NUMSA v SAA Technical, LAC 2024; Regs reg 9).

Facilitation Regulations reg 2(1) refers to “a notice in terms of regulation 2”; it should refer to the request in regulation 1. The Regulations call themselves the “Facilitation Regulations, 2002”, though published in 2003.
